states.note: A request is in flight. It discloses nothing because it knows nothing yet, and a surface that renders a skeleton shaped like the answer it expects is guessing at data it has not received.

The response arrived and held no items. It is deliberately not distinguishable from a page every one of whose entries the viewer is unauthorized to see, because a count of what was filtered is a disclosure of what was filtered.

Rendered on the blocker's own surfaces so they can see the block is in force. On every other surface the subject is simply absent, because a marker where a person used to be tells the blocked party they were blocked.

A private subject and a blocked one look identical to an unauthorized viewer. That is the point: two distinguishable refusals let a viewer determine which one applies, and one of them is a fact about a relationship the other party did not disclose.

The held data is older than the public_cache_stale_seconds budget in packages/schemas/policy-defaults-v1.json. A leaderboard rendered from a superseded generation says which generation it is showing rather than pretending to be current, because D-212 makes a superseded generation readable through the cursor that names it.

A correction, a moderation reversal or a projection rebuild invalidated an inbox item. The item is replaced rather than deleted, because a notification that silently disappears leaves the recipient believing something that is no longer true.

The appellant's own surface, so the detail is theirs. `screening` is absent deliberately: the binding table marks it internal because an automated pre-review pass is not a decision and gives the appellant nothing to act on, so they see `submitted` until a human is assigned.

Shown to every live session the moment a case opens, which is what gives a participant who still has access the chance to cancel it inside the cooling-off window. It names the window and the cancel route and never which factor was presented, because that would tell an attacker which factor to attack next.
